 Youth Vote Powered Democratic Wins 
 After a campaign for on-campus early voting sites and marches to the polls, college students made a difference in close races. 
 by 
 Sayaka Matsuoka 
 November 18, 2026 November 18, 2026

 N.C. A&T's on-campus voting site, where students showed up to vote in greater numbers Tuesday than for the 2024 presidential election. (Carolyn de Berry for The Assembly) 
 Three hundred and thirty-one. That’s how many votes by which Democrat Chuck Hubbard currently leads incumbent Republican Virginia Foxx in North Carolina’s 5th Congressional district. Many were shocked when this historically safe Republican district, a seat held by the GOP for more than 30 years, appeared to flip on election night.
 “Everything that we saw in the weeks up coming to the election showed it was going to be a close election,” Hubbard told The Assembly , “And we felt like the momentum was ours.” 
 Foxx requested a recount and filed for candidacy for the 2028 election on Monday. In office since 2005, Foxx has served as the chair of the House Rules Committee since last year, and as a ranking member of the House Committee on Education and Labor from 2019-23. But as districts turned blue across the country on Election Day, one bloc in particular appeared to make big waves.
 Students from A&T and UNC Greensboro “really came out,” Hubbard said, in part because they were denied on-campus polling places in this midterm election. Hubbard called that “a direct attempt to suppress their vote.”

 “Me and Shia could probably count 99 people that we helped get involved in this process in a single day in the past year,” said Olu Rouse, an NC A&T State University senior and co-founder of Protect Ours, a civic engagement group on campus. “I think we’ve been working at this for almost a year now.”
 Twenty-seven percent of young people—aged 18-29—voted in this year’s midterm elections, according to the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) at Tufts University. That’s the second-highest midterm youth voter turnout in the past 30 years, behind only the 2018 midterms. 
 Locally and nationwide, university and college students spent months fighting for on-campus early-voting sites. When those efforts failed earlier this year , it lit a fire under them, students said.
 “I think students were underestimated, and people paid for it,” said Shia Rozier, a senior at A&T and co-founder of Protect Ours. 
 While students across the state have worked on voter engagement for months, experts say young voters are not a monolith. They are, however, a powerful voting bloc that has historically been ignored or taken for granted.
 “The youth vote is up for grabs,” said Yael Bromberg, a voting-rights expert and adjunct law professor at American University in Washington, D.C. “They are not to be presumed.”
 Getting Activated
 Guilford County experienced a huge college voter turnout increase this year compared to the previous midterm election.
 For voters assigned to the UNCG precinct, early voting was up 86% compared to 2022. For A&T, it was up 72%.
 Total votes—including early votes, absentee, provisional ballots, and Election Day votes—were up, too. For UNCG, total votes cast were up 154% this year compared to 2022. For voters assigned to A&T, they were up 55%.

 “This is true across the board nationally as well,” said Caroline Smith, director of programs at the Andrew Goodman Foundation, a national nonprofit that engages young voters. “We were getting reports from campuses around the country that early voting on their campuses or in their communities had high turnout.”
 Students at both A&T and UNCG worked for months to get an early-voting site on their respective campuses. When the Guilford County Board of Elections voted not to include an early-voting site at either university, students said it energized the campuses.
 Students like Rouse and Rozier planned events like the Oct. 15 and Oct. 22 marches from A&T’s campus to Union Square , an early-voting site 30 minutes away that the Board of Elections added as a “compromise.” Organizers estimate the marches drew more than the entire margin between Hubbard and Foxx, among other close races.
 “The irony is that when these barriers pop up, young voters get really activated,” Smith said. “They break polling records.”
 Kathy Kirkpatrick, Guilford County Democratic Party chair, said she believes students at local colleges and universities launched a movement.
 “I think the actions by A&T and the initial march they had sparked a lot of action across the country,” Kirkpatrick said. “I think it lit a fire under students everywhere.”
 Kirkpatrick pointed to comments Guilford County Board of Elections Chair Eugene Lester made, saying voting was a privilege, not a right during deliberations about whether or not to include the campuses as early-voting sites earlier this year.
 “That was the impetus for a lot of action here in Guilford County,” Kirkpatrick said. “It was a spark that blew up in [the board’s] faces this year.”
 Chris Meadows, Guilford County Republican Party chair, called the young voters who powered some Democratic upsets “malinformed.”
 “They just don’t understand what they’re voting for,” Meadows said. “They’re voting for handouts which aren’t gonna come.”
 At both UNCG and A&T, students organized voter registration campaigns, pizza parties, and even tactical social media posts.
 Jyanne Guide, a senior at A&T and an Andrew Goodman Campus Ambassador, said she remembers seeing what looked like a “fake news” post circulated on Instagram by A&T students right before the university’s homecoming. It said the event— the campus’ 100th homecoming — was postponed . When students swiped, it actually showed early-voting information.
 Jyanne Guide, a senior at N.C. A&T University, worked to mobilize Aggie voters. (Sayaka Matsuoka for The Assembly ) 
 “I think college students played a role in changing the narrative of what it means to get people excited to vote,” Guide said. “It got people interested more than anything else.”
 For decades, those running for elected office have lamented that youth voters are apathetic or uninformed . But that’s far from the case, experts say.
 ‘Leading the Future Today’
 Young people’s preference for Democratic candidates in this midterm was the greatest of any age group, according to CIRCLE . Across the country, 66% of voters ages 18-29 voted for a Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives compared to 56% of voters ages 30-44. Among voters ages 45-64, it was 51%, and 53% of voters 65 and up.
 That doesn’t mean Democrats can take their support for granted, experts said.
 While a little more than half of the students who voted early at UNCG were registered Democrats, about 44% were unaffiliated. At A&T, unaffiliated students made up 42 percent.
 “Young people for a long time have been eschewing traditional institutional affiliations, including affiliations of political parties,” said Bromberg.
 Yael Bromberg, a voting-rights expert and Adjunct Professor of Law at American University Washington College of Law. (Courtesy photo) 
 Like many other voter demographics this year, the economy and jobs were a priority in the midterms for youth voters. Polling showed voters held incumbent Republicans responsible for their concerns.
 “Young people don’t vote for a party or allegiance to a party or candidate as much as other ages of voters,” Smith said. “They vote on issues.”
 Health care, immigration, and education also topped their list of concerns, according to CIRCLE .
 “[Elected officials] need to show that they will listen to voters and follow through on their promises or young people will have no problem showing up and voting them out,” Smith said.
 Meadows, the Guilford GOP chair, agreed many voters were concerned about the economy. But voting for Democrats isn’t the answer, he said.
 “Raising taxes on corporations and high-income people is bad policy,” Meadows said. “We have some of the most liberal universities in the country in Greensboro. They’re not being taught good economic policy or monetary policy. They listen to far-left professors.”
 Still, he said, the Republican Party needs to do a better job courting young voters.
 Kirkpatrick says she knows there is work ahead for Democrats, too.
 “If we want to hold on and truly earn the youth vote in 2028 and beyond, we need to govern in ways that are going to meet their needs or show that we are working toward their needs,” Kirkpatrick said. “People need lower costs; people need healthcare. We gotta step up and step out and govern in the ways that meet the needs of our people.”
 The diminished sense of party identification among young voters likely accounts for the massive shift in this year’s election, experts said.
 In 2024, 56% of young men voted for Trump. This year, the numbers almost completely flipped, with 59% of young men voting for a Democratic U.S. House candidate, according to CIRCLE .
 “Our population cared more about making informed votes,” Guide said. “Like, who am I voting for and what are their policies? That’s the biggest difference I could tell.”
 Social media, the economy, climate change, and reproductive and voting rights all informed the youth vote, experts said.
 Caroline Smith, director of programs at the Andrew Goodman Foundation. (Courtesy photo) 
 “Young people are the ones who will feel the impact of these things long term,” Smith said.
 As youth voters get older and enter the workforce, Meadows said, they’ll vote differently.
 “As people get jobs and they see taxes taken out of their paychecks or their property taxes skyrocketing, then they’ll start voting to make changes,” Meadows said. “We’ll see in two years.”
 Whichever way they vote, students and political experts agree this generation is one of the most civically engaged groups.
 “The results we see prove that,” Guide said.
 Kirkpatrick, who attended local board of elections meetings alongside many of the student leaders this year, said she was moved by their tenacity.
 “It was just a sight to behold,” she said. “It brought me to tears. It was just magical. I’m so impressed by the young people we have in our colleges.”
 Organizations and candidates across the country work to court youth voters in the lead-up to an election, but that’s not how it should be. The youth vote should no longer be an afterthought or seen as just another voting bloc, students said.
 “We’re not just the future leaders of tomorrow,” Rozier said. “We’re leading the future today.”

 Sayaka Matsuoka
